mechanism: NSAIDs inhibit platelet function and damage GI mucosa; warfarin inhibits clotting factors
effect: Greatly increased risk of GI bleeding and haemorrhage
management: Avoid combination. Use paracetamol for analgesia. If NSAID essential, add PPI and monitor INR closely.

mechanism: Dual antiplatelet and anticoagulant effect; aspirin damages GI mucosa
management: Only combine if clear indication (e.g. mechanical valve). Add PPI. Monitor INR.

mechanism: Antibiotics alter gut flora reducing vitamin K synthesis
effect: INR may rise, increasing bleeding risk
management: Monitor INR more frequently during antibiotic course. Adjust warfarin dose as needed.

mechanism: Fluconazole is a potent CYP2C9 inhibitor, blocking warfarin metabolism
effect: Markedly elevated INR and high bleeding risk
management: Reduce warfarin dose by 25-50%. Monitor INR at days 3-5. Consider alternative antifungal.

mechanism: Metronidazole inhibits CYP2C9 and reduces warfarin clearance
effect: Significantly raised INR and bleeding risk
management: Reduce warfarin dose empirically. Check INR at day 3. Use shortest course possible.

mechanism: Omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19, which has minor role in warfarin metabolism
management: Monitor INR when starting/stopping PPI. Lansoprazole may be safer alternative.

mechanism: Statins share CYP3A4 pathway; some inhibit warfarin metabolism
management: Use lower statin doses. Monitor INR when initiating statin therapy.

mechanism: Carbamazepine is a potent CYP inducer, accelerating warfarin metabolism
effect: Substantially reduced INR and loss of anticoagulant effect
management: Avoid combination. If essential, increase warfarin dose with frequent INR monitoring.

mechanism: Rifampicin is the most potent CYP inducer, massively accelerating warfarin clearance
effect: INR may fall to subtherapeutic within days
management: Avoid if possible. If essential, may need 2-3x warfarin dose with daily INR monitoring.

mechanism: Cranberry flavonoids may inhibit CYP2C9
management: Limit cranberry intake. Monitor INR if regular consumption.

mechanism: Ciprofloxacin inhibits CYP1A2 and alters gut flora
management: Monitor INR within 3-5 days of starting. Reduce warfarin dose if needed.

mechanism: Erythromycin inhibits CYP3A4
management: Use azithromycin as alternative. If essential, monitor INR closely.

mechanism: Complex bidirectional interaction — initially inhibits then induces warfarin metabolism; warfarin displaces phenytoin
effect: Unpredictable INR changes; phenytoin toxicity possible
management: Avoid combination. If essential, monitor both INR and phenytoin levels frequently.

mechanism: ACEi reduces aldosterone, decreasing renal potassium excretion
management: Avoid routine K+ supplementation with ACEi. Monitor serum potassium regularly.

mechanism: Both reduce renal potassium excretion via RAAS inhibition
effect: Significant hyperkalaemia risk, especially in renal impairment
management: Monitor K+ within 1 week of starting. Avoid if eGFR <30. Use low-dose spironolactone (25mg).

mechanism: NSAIDs reduce renal prostaglandins causing sodium/water retention and reduced GFR
effect: Reduced antihypertensive effect, AKI risk, hyperkalaemia
management: Use paracetamol instead. If NSAID essential, monitor U&E and BP. Short course only.

mechanism: Trimethoprim blocks ENaC in collecting duct, reducing potassium excretion
effect: Hyperkalaemia, especially in elderly and renal impairment
management: Check K+ before and 5 days after starting. Avoid in eGFR <30.

mechanism: ACEi reduces renal lithium clearance by reducing GFR and increasing proximal reabsorption
management: Avoid combination if possible. If essential, reduce lithium dose and monitor levels weekly.

mechanism: Iodinated contrast can cause AKI; metformin accumulates in renal impairment
effect: Lactic acidosis risk if AKI develops post-contrast
management: Withhold metformin on day of contrast and 48h after. Check eGFR before restarting.

mechanism: Both inhibit gluconeogenesis and alcohol impairs lactate metabolism
effect: Hypoglycaemia and increased lactic acidosis risk
management: Advise moderate alcohol intake. Avoid binge drinking. Monitor blood glucose.

mechanism: Additive glucose-lowering; SGLT2i causes osmotic diuresis which may affect renal function
management: Monitor renal function. Adjust doses in elderly. Ensure adequate hydration.

mechanism: Amiodarone inhibits P-glycoprotein and renal tubular secretion of digoxin
effect: Digoxin toxicity — nausea, bradycardia, arrhythmias, yellow vision
management: Halve digoxin dose when starting amiodarone. Monitor digoxin level at 1 week.

mechanism: Verapamil inhibits P-glycoprotein and renal clearance of digoxin; additive AV nodal block
effect: Digoxin toxicity and severe bradycardia/heart block
management: Reduce digoxin dose by 50%. Monitor HR and digoxin levels. Consider alternative.

mechanism: Clarithromycin inhibits P-glycoprotein and CYP3A4, reducing digoxin clearance
management: Use azithromycin as alternative. If essential, monitor digoxin levels.

mechanism: Furosemide causes hypokalaemia which sensitises myocardium to digoxin
effect: Increased digoxin toxicity risk at therapeutic levels
management: Monitor K+ and Mg2+. Supplement if low. Consider K+-sparing diuretic.

mechanism: Spironolactone reduces renal clearance of digoxin
management: Monitor digoxin level. Beneficial in HF (mortality benefit) so often used together with monitoring.

mechanism: Amlodipine inhibits CYP3A4, reducing statin metabolism
effect: Increased simvastatin exposure and myopathy/rhabdomyolysis risk
management: Limit simvastatin to 20mg with amlodipine. Consider atorvastatin or rosuvastatin instead.

mechanism: Clarithromycin is a potent CYP3A4 inhibitor
effect: Major increase in statin levels; rhabdomyolysis risk
management: Suspend statin during clarithromycin course. Use azithromycin if possible.

mechanism: Grapefruit inhibits intestinal CYP3A4
effect: Increased statin bioavailability and myopathy risk
management: Avoid large quantities of grapefruit. Consider rosuvastatin (not CYP3A4 substrate).

mechanism: Ciclosporin inhibits CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein
effect: Markedly increased statin levels; high rhabdomyolysis risk
management: Avoid simvastatin. Use pravastatin or low-dose rosuvastatin if statin needed.

mechanism: Diltiazem inhibits CYP3A4
management: Limit simvastatin to 20mg. Consider switching to atorvastatin.

mechanism: CYP3A4 inhibition by clarithromycin
management: Pause atorvastatin during treatment or use azithromycin.

mechanism: NSAIDs reduce renal prostaglandins, decreasing lithium clearance
effect: Lithium toxicity — tremor, ataxia, renal failure, seizures
management: Avoid NSAIDs. Use paracetamol. If essential, monitor lithium level within 5 days.

mechanism: Thiazides increase proximal sodium (and lithium) reabsorption
management: Avoid combination. If essential, reduce lithium dose by 50% and monitor levels weekly.

mechanism: Loop diuretics cause sodium depletion, increasing lithium reabsorption
effect: Elevated lithium levels and toxicity risk
management: Monitor lithium levels within 5-7 days. Ensure adequate hydration.

mechanism: Additive neurotoxicity; carbamazepine may enhance lithium CNS effects
effect: Neurotoxicity — tremor, ataxia, confusion — even at therapeutic levels
management: Monitor for neurotoxic symptoms. Check both drug levels.

mechanism: Both are folate antagonists; trimethoprim reduces renal clearance of methotrexate
effect: Pancytopenia, mucositis, potentially fatal bone marrow suppression
management: Avoid combination. Use alternative antibiotic. If given inadvertently, check FBC urgently.

mechanism: NSAIDs reduce renal clearance of methotrexate
management: Avoid NSAIDs within 24h of high-dose MTX. Low-dose MTX: use with caution, monitor FBC.

mechanism: PPIs may reduce renal tubular secretion of methotrexate
effect: Delayed MTX clearance and increased toxicity risk
management: Withhold PPI during high-dose MTX. Low-dose: monitor FBC.

mechanism: Omeprazole inhibits CYP2C19, reducing conversion of clopidogrel to active metabolite
effect: Reduced antiplatelet effect; increased thrombotic risk
management: Use lansoprazole or pantoprazole instead (weaker CYP2C19 inhibition).

mechanism: Dual antiplatelet effect
effect: Increased bleeding risk (but often intentional post-ACS)
management: Indicated post-ACS/PCI for defined duration. Add PPI for GI protection.

mechanism: Both increase serotonin; tramadol inhibits serotonin reuptake
effect: Serotonin syndrome — agitation, clonus, hyperthermia, tachycardia
management: Avoid combination. Use alternative analgesic (morphine, codeine).

mechanism: Massive serotonin accumulation from dual blockade of serotonin breakdown and reuptake
management: Absolutely contraindicated. 2-week washout required between drugs (5 weeks for fluoxetine).

mechanism: Both increase serotonergic activity
effect: Theoretical serotonin syndrome risk (low in practice)
management: Can be used together with monitoring. Advise patient to report agitation, tremor, clonus.

mechanism: SSRIs impair platelet aggregation; some inhibit CYP2C9
management: Add PPI. Monitor INR when starting/stopping SSRI.

mechanism: SSRIs deplete platelet serotonin; NSAIDs damage GI mucosa
management: Add PPI if combination necessary. Consider paracetamol instead.

mechanism: Amiodarone inhibits CYP3A4
management: Limit simvastatin to 20mg. Consider pravastatin or rosuvastatin.

mechanism: Additive negative chronotropic and dromotropic effects
effect: Severe bradycardia, heart block, cardiac arrest
management: Monitor HR and ECG closely. Use lowest effective doses. Consider pacemaker backup.

mechanism: Additive AV nodal suppression; amiodarone inhibits CYP3A4
management: Avoid combination. If essential, intensive cardiac monitoring required.

mechanism: Amiodarone inhibits CYP2C9; phenytoin induces amiodarone metabolism
management: Reduce phenytoin dose by 50%. Monitor phenytoin levels.

mechanism: Ciprofloxacin inhibits CYP1A2, the main metabolic pathway of theophylline
management: Avoid combination. If essential, halve theophylline dose and monitor levels.

mechanism: Ciprofloxacin inhibits CYP1A2
effect: Marked increase in tizanidine levels — hypotension, sedation
management: Contraindicated. Use alternative antibiotic or muscle relaxant.

mechanism: Polyvalent cations chelate ciprofloxacin in the gut
management: Separate doses by 2h (cipro first) or 6h (antacid first).

mechanism: Ciprofloxacin may reduce renal tubular secretion of methotrexate
management: Monitor methotrexate levels and FBC. Consider alternative antibiotic.

mechanism: Additive negative inotropic and chronotropic effects
management: Common combination in practice but start low. Monitor HR and BP.

mechanism: Amlodipine may increase ciclosporin levels; ciclosporin may increase amlodipine levels
effect: Enhanced toxicity of both drugs — gingival hyperplasia, nephrotoxicity
management: Monitor ciclosporin levels. Check renal function. Use alternative CCB if needed.

mechanism: Both are ototoxic; furosemide may increase gentamicin accumulation in inner ear
management: Avoid if possible. If essential, monitor gentamicin levels and audiometry. Adequate hydration.

mechanism: Additive nephrotoxicity
management: Monitor renal function daily. Ensure trough levels of both are within range. Adequate hydration.

mechanism: NSAIDs reduce renal blood flow, impairing aminoglycoside clearance
management: Avoid NSAIDs during aminoglycoside therapy. Monitor renal function.

mechanism: Valproate displaces phenytoin from albumin and inhibits its metabolism; phenytoin induces valproate metabolism
effect: Phenytoin toxicity initially; later reduced valproate levels
management: Monitor free phenytoin levels (not total). Adjust valproate dose.

mechanism: Phenytoin induces CYP3A4, accelerating oestrogen/progesterone metabolism
management: Use high-dose pill (50mcg EE) or non-oral contraception (IUD, depot). Advise barrier method too.

mechanism: Carbamazepine induces CYP3A4, accelerating hormonal metabolism
management: Use IUD or depot medroxyprogesterone. Oral contraceptives unreliable.

mechanism: Erythromycin inhibits CYP3A4, blocking carbamazepine metabolism
management: Avoid erythromycin. Use azithromycin (no CYP3A4 interaction).

mechanism: Verapamil inhibits CYP3A4; carbamazepine induces CYP3A4
management: Avoid combination. Use alternative anticonvulsant or antihypertensive.

mechanism: Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, blocking azathioprine/6-MP metabolism
effect: Life-threatening pancytopenia and bone marrow suppression
management: Reduce azathioprine to 25% of usual dose. Monitor FBC weekly for 8 weeks. Consider mercaptopurine dose titration.

mechanism: Allopurinol inhibits xanthine oxidase, the main metabolic pathway
management: Reduce 6-MP dose to 25-33%. Intensive FBC monitoring.

mechanism: Allopurinol may inhibit warfarin metabolism
management: Monitor INR when starting allopurinol. May need warfarin dose reduction.

mechanism: Both damage GI mucosa; additive ulcerogenic effect
effect: Increased peptic ulcer and GI bleeding risk
management: Add PPI. Avoid prolonged combination. Use paracetamol if possible.

mechanism: Corticosteroids cause insulin resistance and hyperglycaemia
management: Monitor blood glucose frequently. May need to increase metformin or add insulin temporarily.

mechanism: Corticosteroids cause insulin resistance
effect: Significant hyperglycaemia requiring insulin dose increase
management: Increase insulin dose (often 20-50%). Monitor glucose QDS. Variable-rate insulin if severe.

mechanism: Additive negative inotropic and chronotropic effects at AV node
effect: Severe bradycardia, heart block, asystole, cardiogenic shock
management: Avoid IV combination absolutely. Oral combination only with extreme caution and monitoring.

mechanism: Beta-blockers mask hypoglycaemia symptoms (tremor, tachycardia) and impair glycogenolysis
effect: Prolonged hypoglycaemia with masked warning signs
management: Use cardioselective beta-blocker (bisoprolol). Educate patient on non-adrenergic hypo symptoms (sweating).

mechanism: Withdrawal of either causes rebound hypertension; beta-blockers block compensatory vasodilation
effect: Severe rebound hypertension crisis if clonidine stopped
management: If stopping, withdraw clonidine gradually over 1 week before tapering beta-blocker.

mechanism: Diclofenac may block aspirin's irreversible COX-1 binding; both damage GI mucosa
effect: Reduced cardioprotection from aspirin; increased GI bleeding
management: Give aspirin 30min before diclofenac if both essential. Add PPI. Prefer alternative analgesic.

mechanism: NSAID impairs platelet function; rivaroxaban inhibits factor Xa
management: Avoid combination. Use paracetamol. If essential, shortest course with PPI.

mechanism: Carbamazepine induces CYP3A4 and P-gp, accelerating rivaroxaban clearance
effect: Subtherapeutic rivaroxaban levels; increased thrombotic risk
management: Avoid combination. Consider warfarin (can be monitored with INR) or alternative anticonvulsant.

mechanism: Ketoconazole inhibits both CYP3A4 and P-glycoprotein
effect: Markedly increased rivaroxaban levels and bleeding risk
management: Contraindicated. Use alternative antifungal.

mechanism: Rifampicin induces CYP3A4 and P-gp
effect: Substantially reduced apixaban levels; thrombotic risk
management: Avoid combination. Use warfarin with INR monitoring if rifampicin essential.

mechanism: Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4 and P-gp
effect: Increased apixaban levels and bleeding risk
management: Use azithromycin instead. If essential, monitor for bleeding. Short courses preferable.

mechanism: Erythromycin inhibits CYP1A2 and CYP3A4
management: Avoid erythromycin. Use azithromycin. If essential, reduce theophylline dose and monitor levels.

mechanism: Phenytoin induces theophylline metabolism; theophylline reduces phenytoin absorption
management: Monitor both drug levels. Increase doses as needed.

mechanism: Fluoxetine inhibits CYP2D6 (reducing tramadol efficacy) and both increase serotonin
effect: Serotonin syndrome risk; reduced analgesic effect
management: Avoid tramadol. Use morphine, oxycodone, or non-opioid alternatives.

mechanism: Fluoxetine strongly inhibits CYP2D6, blocking tamoxifen activation to endoxifen
effect: Reduced tamoxifen efficacy; potential breast cancer recurrence
management: Switch to citalopram, escitalopram, or venlafaxine (weaker CYP2D6 inhibition).

mechanism: Fluoxetine inhibits CYP2D6 which metabolises metoprolol
effect: Increased metoprolol levels; excessive bradycardia and hypotension
management: Monitor HR and BP. Consider dose reduction of metoprolol or switch to atenolol.

mechanism: Sertraline inhibits CYP2D6/3A4; increased pimozide levels
effect: QT prolongation, torsades de pointes, sudden death
management: Contraindicated. Use alternative antipsychotic.

mechanism: Paroxetine strongly inhibits CYP2D6, blocking codeine conversion to morphine
effect: Loss of analgesic effect from codeine
management: Use alternative analgesic (morphine, paracetamol). Codeine is a prodrug requiring CYP2D6.

mechanism: Both inhibit serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake
management: Avoid combination. Use non-serotonergic analgesic.

mechanism: Divalent cations chelate tetracyclines in gut
management: Separate administration by at least 2 hours.

mechanism: Doxycycline may inhibit warfarin metabolism and alter gut flora
management: Monitor INR during course. Adjust warfarin as needed.

mechanism: Theoretical alteration of gut flora affecting enterohepatic circulation
management: Current guidance: no additional precautions needed for short courses.

mechanism: Calcium chelates levothyroxine in gut, reducing absorption
management: Separate by at least 4 hours. Take levothyroxine on empty stomach.

mechanism: Iron chelates levothyroxine, reducing absorption
management: Separate by at least 4 hours. Check TSH 6 weeks after any change.

mechanism: PPIs raise gastric pH, reducing levothyroxine dissolution and absorption
management: Take levothyroxine 30min before PPI. May need dose increase. Monitor TSH.

mechanism: Calcium reduces bisphosphonate absorption
management: Take alendronate on empty stomach. Separate calcium by at least 30 minutes.

mechanism: Both irritate upper GI mucosa
effect: Increased risk of oesophageal ulceration and GI bleeding
management: Add PPI. Avoid NSAIDs if possible. Ensure correct alendronate technique (upright, water, fasting).

mechanism: Both reduce renal potassium excretion
effect: Severe hyperkalaemia, especially in elderly/renal impairment
management: Check K+ before and 5 days after starting. Avoid in eGFR <30.

mechanism: Both reduce renal potassium excretion via RAAS inhibition
management: Monitor K+ within 1 week. Low-dose spironolactone (25mg) preferred.

mechanism: Both are ototoxic; furosemide increases aminoglycoside cochlear accumulation
management: Avoid if possible. Monitor gentamicin levels and renal function.

mechanism: NSAIDs inhibit renal prostaglandins, reducing diuretic effect
effect: Reduced diuresis, fluid retention, AKI risk
management: Avoid NSAIDs. Use paracetamol. If essential, monitor weight, U&E, and diuretic response.

mechanism: Beta-blockers mask hypoglycaemia symptoms and impair counter-regulatory response
management: Use cardioselective beta-blocker. Educate on hypo symptoms.

mechanism: Steroids cause insulin resistance and hepatic gluconeogenesis
management: Increase insulin dose. Monitor glucose QDS. May need variable-rate insulin.

mechanism: Additive glucose lowering; TZDs cause fluid retention
management: Reduce insulin dose when adding TZD. Monitor for peripheral oedema and heart failure symptoms.

mechanism: Ciprofloxacin inhibits CYP1A2, the main metabolic pathway of clozapine
effect: Clozapine toxicity — seizures, sedation, hypotension, agranulocytosis
management: Contraindicated. Use alternative antibiotic. If essential, reduce clozapine by 50% and monitor levels.

mechanism: Carbamazepine induces CYP1A2; both may cause agranulocytosis
effect: Reduced clozapine levels AND additive bone marrow suppression
management: Contraindicated due to additive agranulocytosis risk.

mechanism: Smoking induces CYP1A2; stopping smoking removes this induction
effect: Clozapine levels may double within days of stopping, causing toxicity
management: Reduce clozapine dose by 25-50% when patient stops smoking. Monitor levels closely.

mechanism: Ondansetron is a 5-HT3 antagonist that may reduce tramadol's serotonergic analgesic component
management: Use alternative antiemetic (metoclopramide, cyclizine) or alternative analgesic.

mechanism: Both prolong QT interval
effect: Increased risk of torsades de pointes
management: Monitor QTc. Avoid if QTc >500ms. Use metoclopramide or cyclizine instead.

mechanism: Both prolong QT interval; erythromycin inhibits CYP3A4
effect: QT prolongation, ventricular arrhythmias, sudden death
management: Avoid combination. Use metoclopramide or alternative antibiotic.

mechanism: Ketoconazole inhibits CYP3A4 and both prolong QT
effect: Markedly elevated domperidone levels; arrhythmia risk
management: Contraindicated. Use alternative antifungal.

mechanism: Additive QT prolongation
management: Avoid combination. Monitor ECG if essential. Use azithromycin instead.

mechanism: Additive neurotoxicity
effect: Encephalopathic syndrome — confusion, tremor, EPS, fever
management: Monitor closely for neurotoxic signs. Use lowest effective doses.

mechanism: Metoclopramide is a dopamine antagonist, blocking levodopa's therapeutic effect
management: Contraindicated in Parkinson disease. Use domperidone (doesn't cross BBB well) for nausea.

mechanism: Additive CNS and respiratory depression
management: Avoid combination. If essential, use lowest effective doses with close monitoring. FDA black box warning.

mechanism: Additive CNS depression; gabapentin may increase morphine absorption
management: Start gabapentin at low dose. Monitor sedation and respiratory rate.

mechanism: Additive CNS and respiratory depression
management: Avoid combination. If palliative, use lowest effective doses with monitoring.

mechanism: Paroxetine strongly inhibits CYP2D6, preventing codeine activation
management: Use alternative analgesic. Codeine requires CYP2D6 for activation.

mechanism: Ibuprofen may competitively block aspirin's irreversible COX-1 binding site on platelets
management: Take aspirin at least 30min before ibuprofen. Prefer alternative analgesic.

mechanism: Dual antiplatelet effect
effect: Increased bleeding risk (often intentional after ACS/PCI)
management: Co-prescribe PPI for GI protection when used together.

mechanism: Aspirin reduces renal clearance of methotrexate
management: Avoid with high-dose MTX. Low-dose: monitor FBC and U&E.

mechanism: Both are nephrotoxic; NSAIDs reduce renal blood flow
management: Avoid NSAIDs. Use paracetamol. Monitor renal function if NSAID essential.

mechanism: Ciclosporin causes potassium retention in the distal tubule
management: Avoid K+ supplements. Monitor serum potassium regularly.

mechanism: Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4 and P-gp
management: Avoid. Use azithromycin. Monitor tacrolimus trough if essential.

mechanism: Fluconazole inhibits CYP3A4
management: Reduce tacrolimus dose by 50%. Monitor levels closely.

mechanism: Both may prolong QT interval
management: Monitor ECG. Check baseline QTc. Avoid if QTc >500ms.

mechanism: Both are antifolate agents
management: Absolutely avoid. Use alternative antibiotic.

mechanism: Trimethoprim reduces renal tubular secretion of digoxin
management: Monitor digoxin level. Consider dose reduction.

mechanism: Sulfasalazine inhibits folate absorption; additive antifolate effect
management: Ensure adequate folic acid supplementation. Monitor FBC regularly.

mechanism: Both cause vasodilation via cGMP pathway
management: Absolutely contraindicated. 24h gap after sildenafil (48h after tadalafil) before nitrates.

mechanism: Additive vasodilation
management: Start alpha-blocker first at stable dose. Begin sildenafil at 25mg.

mechanism: Non-selective beta-blockers antagonise beta-2 receptors in bronchi
management: Contraindicated in asthma. Use cardioselective beta-blocker (bisoprolol) if essential.

mechanism: Additive negative inotropic and chronotropic effects
effect: Severe bradycardia, heart block, heart failure
management: Avoid. If essential, intensive cardiac monitoring.

mechanism: Combined withdrawal causes rebound hypertension
management: Withdraw clonidine gradually. Taper beta-blocker after clonidine stopped.

mechanism: Dual RAAS blockade reduces potassium excretion
management: Monitor K+ within 1 week. Use 25mg spironolactone max. Avoid if eGFR <30.

mechanism: Triple RAAS blockade
management: Contraindicated, especially in diabetes. Avoid dual/triple RAAS blockade.

mechanism: ARBs reduce aldosterone, decreasing K+ excretion
management: Avoid routine K+ supplements. Monitor serum potassium.

mechanism: NSAIDs reduce renal prostaglandins
management: Avoid NSAIDs. Monitor U&E if essential.

mechanism: Additive glucose lowering; pioglitazone causes fluid retention
management: Reduce insulin when adding pioglitazone. Monitor for oedema and weight gain.

mechanism: Fluconazole inhibits CYP2C9 (main metabolic pathway of gliclazide)
management: Monitor blood glucose closely. Reduce gliclazide dose. Consider shorter antifungal course.

mechanism: Fluoroquinolones can cause dysglycaemia independently
management: Monitor blood glucose more frequently during antibiotic course.

mechanism: Phenobarbital induces CYP3A4
management: Use non-oral contraception (IUD, depot). Oral contraceptives unreliable.

mechanism: Rifampicin is the most potent CYP3A4 inducer
management: Use non-hormonal contraception during and 4 weeks after rifampicin.

mechanism: Rifampicin massively induces CYP3A4
effect: Subtherapeutic PI levels; HIV treatment failure
management: Contraindicated with most PIs. Use rifabutin instead at reduced dose.

mechanism: Ketoconazole inhibits CYP3A4
management: Avoid combination. If sedation needed, use lorazepam (glucuronidated, not CYP).

mechanism: Isoniazid induces CYP2E1, increasing toxic NAPQI metabolite
management: Limit paracetamol to 2g/day during isoniazid therapy. Monitor LFTs.

mechanism: Isoniazid inhibits CYP2C19, reducing phenytoin metabolism (especially slow acetylators)
management: Monitor phenytoin levels. Reduce dose in slow acetylators.

mechanism: Valproate inhibits lamotrigine glucuronidation
effect: Doubled lamotrigine levels; Stevens-Johnson syndrome risk
management: Halve lamotrigine dose with valproate. Very slow titration (25mg every 2 weeks).

mechanism: Carbamazepine induces valproate metabolism; valproate inhibits carbamazepine epoxide hydrolase
effect: Reduced valproate levels; increased carbamazepine-epoxide toxicity
management: Monitor levels of both. Watch for carbamazepine toxicity symptoms.

mechanism: Haloperidol blocks dopamine receptors, directly opposing levodopa's mechanism
effect: Worsening Parkinsonism; neuroleptic malignant syndrome risk
management: Avoid typical antipsychotics in Parkinson disease. Use quetiapine or clozapine if antipsychotic needed.

mechanism: Iron chelates levodopa in the gut
management: Separate by at least 2 hours. Take levodopa on empty stomach.

mechanism: Additive vasodilation via alpha-blockade and PDE5 inhibition
management: Start sildenafil at 25mg. Take at different times of day. Counsel on postural symptoms.

mechanism: Additive hypotension from dual vasodilation
management: Stabilise on alpha-blocker first. Start PDE5 inhibitor at lowest dose.

mechanism: Clarithromycin inhibits CYP3A4 and P-gp, reducing colchicine clearance
management: Avoid combination. If essential in normal renal function, reduce colchicine dose and use short course.

mechanism: Ciclosporin inhibits P-glycoprotein efflux of colchicine
management: Avoid combination. If essential, reduce colchicine dose substantially.

mechanism: Verapamil inhibits P-glycoprotein
effect: Increased dabigatran levels and bleeding risk
management: Reduce dabigatran to 110mg BD. Take simultaneously. Monitor for bleeding.

mechanism: Rifampicin induces P-glycoprotein
management: Avoid combination. Use warfarin with INR monitoring instead.

mechanism: Dronedarone inhibits P-glycoprotein
management: Reduce edoxaban dose to 30mg daily. Monitor for bleeding.

mechanism: Miconazole inhibits CYP2C9, the main metabolic pathway of most sulfonylureas
management: Avoid oral/gel miconazole with sulfonylureas. Monitor glucose closely.

mechanism: Beta-blockers allow unopposed alpha-stimulation by adrenaline
management: In anaphylaxis with beta-blocker: may need IV glucagon. Higher adrenaline doses may be needed.
